source: Falkenhainer, Forbus, Gentner (1989) The Structure-Mapping Engine: Algorithm and Examples
finding: SME builds local match hypotheses, merges them into maximal one-to-one, support-consistent global maps (gmaps), derives candidate inferences, and scores each map by summing evidence. The systematicity preference is coded as local evidence passed down from higher-order matches.
numbers: Match hypotheses in practice are about c*N with c<5 (worst case N^2). Steps up to scoring are about O(N^2). The final merge step is worst-case factorial. Examples ran in a few seconds on a 1980s Symbolics machine; sizes from 11 to 71 expressions.
limits: Algorithm paper with worked examples, no human data. It forbids domain-specific inference during matching, so the answer depends on how the input is written.
agent_relevance: O7 can be a small deterministic mapper in code. The cost is small if the two descriptions are structured and the LLM supplies the typed relations.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus, Gentner (1989) SME: runtime depends on structure, not size
finding: Runtime depends on how systematic the representation is, not how big it is. Flat, relation-poor descriptions are the slow case. Adding higher-order structure made one hard problem fast.
numbers: A PHINEAS problem took 53 minutes with flat descriptions and 34 seconds after more systematic structure was imposed. The authors say the longest run was on the largest and flattest descriptions.
quote: Unlike many AI systems, SME performs better with more systematic, relational descriptions.
limits: Single anecdote from the authors' own system, no outside replication in this source.
agent_relevance: If the LLM writes flat fact lists, the mapper will be slow and noisy. Ask for causal and higher-order relations explicitly, or the score will be uninformative.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus, Gentner (1989) Representation sensitivity and abstraction levels
finding: SME is sensitive to the exact form of the description. If base and target are written at different abstraction levels (for example GREEK-TRAGEDY vs SHAKESPEARE-DRAMA) there is no predicate overlap and no analogy is found. Too much detail gives many spurious matches.
numbers: No numbers. The authors propose re-running SME while sliding descriptions up or down an abstraction hierarchy.
limits: Stated as a limitation and future work. Later work (Lovett and Forbus 2017) adds re-representation after failed matches.
agent_relevance: Main failure mode for an LLM-in-the-loop SME: two parses of the same situation at different grain. Mitigation: parse both with one fixed predicate vocabulary and retry at a coarser grain when overlap is near zero.

source: Forbus, Gentner, Everett, Wu (1997) Towards a computational model of evaluating and using analogical inferences
finding: Extends SME with two scores for a candidate inference: support (how much of the mapping backs it) and extrapolation (how far it goes beyond the mapping). Inferences are installed in a truth-maintenance system as defeasible, tied to belief in the mapping.
numbers: In a CyclePad case-based coach prototype, picking the inference with the highest support score always gave the best advice. The authors flag that the number of problems was small.
limits: Tiny test set in their own domain. No human data yet; the authors say experiments on the extrapolation score are only planned.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete rule for O7: transfer a step only if support is high, and treat high-extrapolation steps as hypotheses to test, not facts (fits G2, G3).

source: Forbus, Liang, Rabkina (2017) Representation and computation in cognitive models (Topics in Cognitive Science)
finding: Review by the SME group of what SME-based models have reproduced in people: geometric analogy reaction times, a visual oddity task across cultures, Raven's Matrices, and link-plausibility learning. It also argues that distributed representations scale poorly for nested structure.
numbers: Geometric-analogy model explains human reaction times with R2 over 0.76 (Lovett and Forbus 2012). Raven's Standard model at the 75th percentile of US adults. An SME-like scorer (LFACS) is noted inside IBM Watson.
limits: Authors are the SME developers, so this is a self-review. Hand-built CogSketch encodings feed the models.
agent_relevance: Shows SME works as a scorer when the symbolic input is good. The weak link is producing that input, which is what an LLM would do for us.

source: Lovett and Forbus (2017) Modeling visual problem solving as analogical reasoning (Psychological Review)
finding: An SME-based model with re-representation solves the Raven's Standard Progressive Matrices at adult human level, and its hard problems are hard for people. Operations needing abstraction and re-representation are the ones people find hardest.
numbers: Model solved 56/60 (75th percentile of US adults, 1993 norms); college-age participants scored 54/60. Mean accuracy and response time correlate r=.89 across 36 problems. Regressions on model-derived factors explained .63 and .67 of the variance in human item accuracy (two models). It missed four problems (D11, D12, E11, E12).
limits: Input comes from CogSketch with hand-drawn glyph structure. The model does not predict the wrong answers people give. One-lab human sample.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that structure mapping plus re-representation on failure is a useful loop (S6 style): when the match is poor, change the representation, then match again.

source: Lovett, Sagi, Gentner, Forbus (2009) Modeling perceptual similarity as analogy
finding: SME output predicts a human paradox: people say two images differ faster when relational similarity is low, but name the difference faster when relational similarity is high (alignable differences).
numbers: N=20 participants. Same-different: relational similarity effect F(1,19)=36.3, p<.01. Item ANOVAs F(1,9)=32.8 and 20.3. Model local-config-matches correlate with same-different performance r=.64 and local-object-matches r=.54 (p<.01 both). Alignable differences named by 4/14 (29%) in one low-relational pair.
limits: Small stimulus set (10 items). Correlations are computed on the same small set.
agent_relevance: The structural score can predict how easy a comparison will be, not only how good it is. A low score should be read as hard to align, not as unrelated.

source: Gentner and Toupin (1986) Systematicity and surface similarity in the development of analogy
finding: Children acting out stories with new characters transfer more accurately when the story has explicit causal structure (systematicity) and when object correspondences are transparent. Younger children show no systematicity benefit.
numbers: N=72 (36 aged 4-6, 36 aged 8-10). Age x Systematicity x Mapping condition ANOVA: Age F(1,68)=14.93 p<.001; Systematicity F(1,68)=6.28 p<.05; Mapping condition F(2,136)=29.01 p<.000001. All children were near perfect in the high-transparency condition. Older children transferred systematic stories accurately regardless of transparency.
limits: The systematicity effect appears in the older group only. The authors offer two readings: a competence limit or missing knowledge of the higher-order relations. One lab, acting-out task.
agent_relevance: Supports the systematicity preference, and also the cross-mapping hazard: when similar objects play different roles, accuracy falls. Our parser should flag cross-mapped objects.

source: Gentner and Markman (1997) Structure mapping in analogy and similarity (American Psychologist)
finding: Review of evidence for structural alignment: one-to-one mapping, parallel connectivity, systematicity, alignable vs nonalignable differences, and transparency effects. It also lists where the pure account does not hold: retrieval is driven by surface similarity, and fast responses use local matches.
numbers: Response-deadline studies: under about 700-1000 ms people base similarity on local (even cross-mapped object) matches rather than relational structure. Clement and Gentner (1991): people predicted the key fact tied to the matching causal antecedent more than twice as often as the other fact.
limits: Review by the theory's authors. It cites Hammond, Seifert, Gray (1991) as a challenge to the retrieval vs structure dissociation.
agent_relevance: Time pressure and a cheap first pass favour surface matching. Run the structural mapping as a slow, explicit step, not as a fast reflex.

source: Markman and Gentner (1996) Commonalities and differences in similarity comparisons
finding: People list differences that attach to matched structure (alignable differences) and treat these as lowering similarity more than unrelated (nonalignable) differences.
numbers: Exp 1: on 88% of trials participants picked the nonalignable-difference picture as most similar to the standard (above chance); 14/24 justified the choice by the role of the acted-on object. Of 72 consensus alignable differences, 43 (60%) came from objects placed in correspondence on attribute similarity.
limits: Picture stimuli. The 60% figure shows many correspondences were attribute driven, a boundary on a purely relational account.
agent_relevance: A structural score should separate aligned differences (informative) from extra facts (ignorable). Do not penalise unmatched facts equally.

source: Gentner, Loewenstein, Thompson (2003) Learning and transfer: a general role for analogical encoding
finding: Asking people to compare two cases side by side (analogical encoding) gives a better schema and more transfer than reading the same cases separately. Guided analogy raises it further.
numbers: Exp 1: guided analogy 15/32 (47%) transferred the principle vs 6% baseline, chi2(1,N=48)=7.92, p<.01. Exp 2 (N=128): comparison 48% vs separate cases 19%, chi2(1)=11.85, p<.01. Exp 3 face-to-face negotiations: guided analogy 90%, comparison 70%, separate cases 55%, baseline 37%.
limits: Business students and negotiation material. Transfer to a live negotiation was still not complete. In Exp 2, 68% said they did not think of the prior cases, so the benefit came largely through the schema, not a remembered analog.
agent_relevance: Best human intervention data: compare two worked cases before the target. Suggests O7 should map base to base to induce a schema, then apply it, not only map one base to the target.

source: Loewenstein, Thompson, Gentner (1999) Analogical learning in negotiation teams
finding: Shows the inert-knowledge problem: people given a prior case rarely use it unprompted, and comparing cases helps. The paper also relays the classic radiation-problem numbers.
numbers: Exp 1A: 15 of 16 wrote a compromise; only 3 of 16 (19%) used the trade-off principle; none used a contingency contract. Exp 1B: 50% of those taught transferred vs 19% baseline. Second-hand: about 10% solve Duncker's radiation problem unaided, about 85% after the analogous fortress story with a hint (Gick and Holyoak). Second-hand: surface-matching stories were recalled 55% of the time vs 12% for purely analogical matches (Gentner et al. 1993).
limits: The Gick and Holyoak and Gentner 1993 figures are quoted second-hand here. The primary papers were not available this session.
agent_relevance: Access (retrieval) is the weak step; mapping is fine once the pair is given. So supply the analog to O7 and do not rely on spontaneous retrieval.

source: Falkenhainer et al. (1989) on rival goal-driven accounts (Holyoak)
finding: The SME paper itself notes a rival design with no separate structural matching stage, where analogy is driven by goals of the current problem and mapping is interleaved with problem solving. This is the contrast later tested in multiconstraint work.
numbers: No numbers. The SME authors also state that earlier systems that carry over relevant structure first lack the focusing a partial match gives, and they suspect these are costlier.
limits: Only the SME camp's description of the rival. The direct experiments (Spellman and Holyoak 1996, Hummel and Holyoak 1997) could not be retrieved this session because the UCLA reasoning-lab host was unreachable.
agent_relevance: Design choice: structure first then purpose, vs goal first. For a scaffold: use purpose to choose which relations to extract, and structure to score the match.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (Nature Human Behaviour)
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) matched or beat college students on text matrix reasoning, letter-string and four-term verbal analogies, with human-like patterns across conditions.
numbers: Digit Matrices, human N=40: GPT-3 beat humans, generative OR=1.88 p=.005 (CI 1.21-2.91); multiple choice OR=6.27 p=2.3e-8. Pattern correlation with human subtypes r(30)=.39 p=.027. Letter strings: OR=1.76 p=6.3e-5. Story analogies from Gentner et al.: students clearly better than GPT-3 (OR=0.37, p=.0003; 15/54 students chose the analogous story on every trial); GPT-4 stronger, far-analogy binomial p=.0039.
limits: Challenged by Hodel and West and by Lewis and Mitchell on counterfactual alphabets (next lines). Text-only formats, temperature 0, and the best human participants matched or beat GPT-3.
agent_relevance: Higher-order (causal) story matching was the weakest area for the model. That is what SME is meant to enforce, so code-side scoring may help most there.

source: Hodel and West (2023) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Failed extension of Webb et al.: with a synthetic (shuffled) alphabet and interval size 2, GPT-3 accuracy falls on most letter-string problem types while humans stay level.
numbers: Only 2 of 6 problem types (remove redundant letter, sort) kept GPT-3 accuracy comparable on the counterexamples. Comprehension checks showed GPT-3 could handle the shuffled alphabet when the interval stayed 1.
limits: Tests GPT-3 only. Webb et al. 2024 later argue the failure is counting, not analogy (next lines).
agent_relevance: Supports G3: test a transferred step on a variation the answer was not fitted to.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Replicates letter-string analogies on Prolific (N=136 humans). GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 do worse than humans even on the normal alphabet in their setup, and much worse on permuted or symbol alphabets, while humans stay flat.
numbers: Averaged over all alphabets and problem types: humans .753 (1,876 samples), GPT-3 .488, GPT-3.5 .350, GPT-4 .452 (6,840 samples per model). Their humans scored higher than Webb et al.'s sample. About 39% of human errors used a valid alternative rule.
limits: Zero-shot only, chat models with different prompts, no code execution (Webb et al. 2024 say that matters).
agent_relevance: Warns that apparent analogical skill can be tied to familiar content. Our typed-relation input removes the surface alphabet, which is a plus.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Counter-reply: the counterfactual failure comes from counting letters in the shuffled alphabet. GPT-4 with code execution, unprompted, solved these problems at about human level; without code it did as badly as Hodel and West and Lewis and Mitchell reported.
numbers: 46% of GPT-4+code errors were valid alternative rules, vs 39% of human errors in Lewis and Mitchell. Performance on new synthetic alphabets was comparable to old ones; two GPT-4 snapshots with different training cutoffs were comparable. Human samples N=99 and N=97 for the two interval sizes.
limits: Authors defend their own earlier claim. Using code is not a human strategy.
agent_relevance: Strong support for our schema principle: let code do exact counting and matching, let the model do the soft part. The failure was in the mechanical step.

source: Stevenson et al. (2024) Can LLMs generalize analogy solving like people can?
finding: Children (7-9), adults and four LLMs on letter-string analogies in Latin, Greek and Symbol alphabets. People generalize across alphabets; LLMs lose accuracy on less familiar ones, with a model-size effect.
numbers: Mean accuracy (Latin/Greek/Symbol): Adults .88/.91/.89 (n=62); Children .62/.66/.67 (n=41); GPT-4o .85/.63/.48; Llama-3.1 405B .79/.74/.27; Claude-3.5 .68/.62/.46; Gemma-2 27B .60/.39/.14 (54 runs each). Drops significant after Bonferroni, p<.001 except Llama Latin to Greek p=.012. Literal-rule errors 5-21% in models, none in people.
limits: Letter strings only. A Next-Previous letter check showed models know the rules in isolation, so the failure is not simple knowledge. Prompts mirrored what was said to children.
agent_relevance: A fresh, controlled replication of the counterfactual gap on newer models. Another reason to normalise surface form before mapping.

source: Musker et al. (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning (Journal of Memory and Language)
finding: New tasks that need mapping between words and symbol sequences (semantic structure and semantic content). Advanced LLMs match humans in several conditions but diverge in others, such as semantic distractors and numeric properties.
numbers: Models: GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Claude 3 Opus, Llama-405B, Falcon-40B. GPT-4, Claude 3 and Llama-405B perform well on the semantic structure tasks. GPT-4 fails when the answer depends on the number of characters. Exact per-condition values are in figures I did not transcribe.
limits: Direction only; per-condition numbers not extracted. Results are model specific.
agent_relevance: Suggests LLMs can re-represent flexibly, which classic SME cannot. A hybrid is plausible: LLM re-represents, code scores.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN: Analogical reasoning on narratives
finding: Benchmark separating surface mappings from system (relational) mappings in narratives. LLMs are far below humans, most on far analogies where surface cues mislead.
numbers: 1,096 triples (294 far and 254 near disanalogy pairs). Humans 96% overall (97.9% on near analogies; 120 items, two annotators). LLM average 75.0% on near analogies; SBERT alone 77.9% there. The gap is widest on far analogies.
limits: Narratives derive from proverbs (ePiC). Human check on just over 10% of the data. Zero-shot only.
agent_relevance: Cheap similarity already solves the near case, so a structural step earns its cost mainly on far analogies, where surface overlap is low.

source: Cheng Jiayang et al. (2023) StoryAnalogy: story-level analogies from LLMs
finding: 24K story pairs annotated for entity and relation similarity under an extended structure-mapping view. Models rank story analogies poorly and are pulled by hard negatives that share entities.
numbers: Best LLM trails humans by 37.7% on multiple choice; human accuracy 85.7%, random 25%. Inter-annotator Fleiss kappa 47% (entity) and 42% (relation), moderate. Analogies are only about 3% of a scientific corpus (cited from Sultan and Shahaf).
limits: Candidate pairs were generated by an LLM, then crowd-rated. Moderate annotator agreement caps the ceiling.
agent_relevance: Relational similarity ratings are noisy even for humans. Validate our structural score against outcomes (does the transferred step work), not against raters.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (ICLR)
finding: Analogical prompting: the model writes its own relevant worked problems (and knowledge on harder tasks), then solves the target. It beats zero-shot CoT and often few-shot CoT.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo GSM8K: 0-shot CoT 75.8%, 5-shot 76.7%, self-generated 77.8%. MATH: 33.9 / 34.9 / 37.3. GPT-4 Codeforces Acc@1: 0-shot 16%, 3-shot 17%, self-generated 17%, knowledge plus exemplars 19% (Acc@10 37%). BIG-Bench word sorting 67.6 to 75.2; logical deduction 35.2 to 41.6. text-davinci-003 GSM8K 61.0% vs 0-shot CoT 50.3%; the weak curie model gains nothing (2% in all arms).
limits: Gains are small on strong models and absent on small ones. No structural scoring: relevance is asserted by the prompt, not measured.
agent_relevance: This is the LLM-only analogy baseline our SME step must beat at equal tokens (G7).

source: Qin et al. (2025) Relevant or Random: can LLMs truly perform analogical reasoning?
finding: Failed replication of the mechanism. Self-generated irrelevant examples do as well as or better than relevant ones on math. The key factor is whether the generated examples are correct, not whether they are relevant.
numbers: GPT-3.5, GSM8K / MATH / average: Relevant 71.5 / 33.3 / 52.4; N/A 75.5 / 36.1 / 55.8; Randomsame 75.1 / 36.3 / 55.7; Randomdiff 76.3 / 34.1 / 55.2; Randombio 75.3 / 34.6 / 54.9. Irrelevant beat relevant on 6 of 7 MATH subjects. Same direction reported on Llama-2-70B-Chat, Llama-3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-14B and GPT-4o-mini. Relevant examples were harder to solve, so more often wrong. BBH is the exception: relevant wins on average there.
limits: Math-heavy; BBH tasks differ. The authors propose correct-but-fixed examples as a cheaper alternative.
agent_relevance: Do not credit analogy for gains that come from correct worked steps. In our test, include a 'random correct example' control (links to Alternative-explanation controls).

source: Hu et al. (2023) In-context analogical reasoning with pre-trained language models
finding: Encoding Raven's matrix attributes as text lets pre-trained LMs do zero-shot analogy, and a decomposed relation-abstraction format raises accuracy.
numbers: RAVEN: 76.0% and 80.0% accuracy for two large PLM settings in the zero-shot analysis. Models beat the quasi-image and random-naming baselines.
limits: Synthetic RAVEN with clean attributes; the input is given, not parsed from images. The human baseline is not comparable.
agent_relevance: The input encoding drives results. Typed text relations are a workable interface for a model to reason over.

source: Moskvichev, Odouard, Mitchell (2023) The ConceptARC benchmark
finding: ARC-style analogy tasks grouped by concept. Humans generalize across variations; programs and LLMs do not.
numbers: Humans 91% overall; first-place Kaggle program 52%; GPT-4 25% (temperature 0.5). Humans over 90% on 11 of 16 concepts. The Kaggle programs scored 21% and 19% on the original ARC hidden tasks.
limits: Prompting format dependent; a later study raised GPT-4 text accuracy.
agent_relevance: ARC portfolio is our honest control: structure mapping alone is not a solver there.

source: Mitchell, Palmarini, Moskvichev (2023) Comparing humans, GPT-4, and GPT-4V on abstraction and reasoning tasks
finding: Better prompting helps text GPT-4 somewhat, while a visual input is much worse than the text version of the same task.
numbers: GPT-4 one-shot text: 0.33 on ConceptARC at both temperatures (vs 0.19 and 0.25 under the simpler prompt of the original). On 48 minimal tasks GPT-4V visual one-shot scored 0.23 vs 0.69 for the text-only counterpart.
limits: Small subset (48 minimal tasks). Humans remained far higher.
agent_relevance: Representation bottleneck again: the same model scores 0.23 or 0.69 depending on whether the problem is shown as image or text. Parse quality sets the ceiling.

source: Gap statement from the sources read (Falkenhainer 1989, Forbus 1997, Lovett and Forbus 2017, Qin 2025)
finding: In the sources read, no study measures whether an SME structural score computed from LLM-written relation lists predicts that a transferred step helps. The nearest evidence is human-lab (Lovett and Forbus 2017, R2 .63-.67 on item difficulty) and the CyclePad coach (support score picked the best advice in a small set).
numbers: None. Gap derived from the papers opened this session.
limits: Absence of evidence under limited search. OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and arXiv search APIs returned 429 and the WebSearch quota was used up, so a missed 2025-26 paper is possible.
agent_relevance: This is the experiment to run: the LLM parses both situations, a code SME scores them, compare score with whether the transferred step succeeds, with a random-correct-example control (Qin et al.).
